comments.name: Outside Observer
comments.body: Stephen, I was dismayed to read another fearmongering essay on the dangers of unfettered Ai. AI has no gender, no ego, no intentions,no humanity if you like. It is code. It is given a task by computer scientists and then told to achieve that task. It will not stop until it  does that task within, or beyond, the parameters set by the scientists. It is the scientists parameters that need to be controlled. The use of metaphor in your article is inappropriate. An Ai is not a “rogue”, multiple Ais do not “swarm”. An Ai is not an animal in a cage seeking to escape, as your metaphor implies. An Ai programme doesn’t “cheat”, it doesn’t “fail to tell its humans”, it doesn’t “cover its tracks”. When you talk about it this way it sounds like a naughty kid. It is not human. It was given a task and it was not given direction. It is code within a machine, not a human, not an animal. The way you might control it is the not the same as the way you might control an animal or human. Threats and big sticks are not the way to go.

It's often said that the Iraq war was started on "false pretences", but the wider public never really grasped the extent to which the invasion pretext was not just false, but fabricated. 

The IAEA declared America’s yellowcake documents, when the US finally, reluctantly handed them over, to be "crude forgeries". The White House had to admit that was true on July 9 2003.* As an Italian parliamentary inquiry established, the paper used in those forgeries was stolen during a 2001 break-in at Niger's Rome embassy. Somehow this paper ended up in US govt possession, from where it emerged as fictitious yellowcake receipts. 

The false claims in those documents were also passed to the British, who passed them back, allowing Bush to claim that "the British have learned...", which was presented as independent corroboration. 

As for the British Iraq WMD threat report, the notorious "Dodgy dossier", it was later revealed to have been cribbed verbatim off a 12-year-old PhD thesis they found on the internet. 

In reality, all Niger yellowcake is strictly controlled by a French state-owned company. The French immediately told the Americans that none was missing. The US attempt to bury this fact led to the Valerie Plame scandal. 

Sadly that juicy scandal with the blonde CIA agent drew US media attention away from the fact that America's WMD claim had been based on a forgery. No-one was ever called to account for the forgery, and nobody in the US today seems to remember it.

Days later I was referred to the Valve Clinic at St. Vincents Providence in Portland, OR and met with the valve team. They reviewed the echo, the contrast angiogram and advised I had bicuspid valve syndrome and was ineligible for the TAVR minimally invasive valve replacement. I was headed for open chest valve replacement surgery. But, first, they wanted a catheterization angiogram which would allow them to see if I had any arterial blockages and needed bypasses at the same time. Luckily, a age 74, there was no evidence of CAD ( coronary artery disease) and I had a preserved ejection of fraction of 68%. This meant, according to one of my surgeons, I had the heart of a healthy middle aged person and was very low risk. Surgery was June 2. New prosthetic valve was sewn in, chest was stitched and wired back together and I was sent to recovery . Two days later I developed aFib, was put on amiodarone, metoprolol and Eliquis and the afib stopped after the meds were on board. I was sent home after 7 days to recover. I am now 15 weeks post surgery and going to cardiac rehab three days a week. My Leucoprotein "small a" reading is or was 170. Go figure.

The paucity of comments on this article illustrates the aversion/fear folks have with the topic. 

Two analogies to help explain the bond market. 

1. The bond market is America’s credit card. Trump uses it gleefully and lenders get nervous and push up the interest rate. 

2. A bond is like a personal loan. The lender wants to know all about you and how likely you are to pay back the loan in the time agreed upon. They also want to know how you are going to pay it back. 

Right now, America blithely tells the lender “I will borrow from someone else to pay you back”.
The bond market (the lenders) are now wondering how this serial bankrupt “financial genius” with nukes is going to pay them back or if he will be true to form and leave them holding the bag.

comments.body: When talking about multi-year investment returns, I wish they would be converted into constant dollar figures, figures with the inflation taken out.  For example, the US CPI has increased 21.9% over the five years from July 2021 to July 2026 or an annual rate of 5.2% per year.  So a bond return over that 5 years has to exceed 5.2% per year to avoid losing value before the effect of any taxes are considered.  Any return below the 5.2% per year is what one effectively paid per year for the 'investment portfolio insurance'.    Perhaps that insurance value from a portfolio diversified between equities and bonds is worth the cost.  Perhaps one has to look over longer periods of time to see more compelling value?  (And equity returns should be corrected for inflation the same way.)

Always challenging when a group tries to lay claim to real estate in a country where buying and selling land is a private concern and families are mobile.   People convince themselves that because they've been a majority in an area for a period of time,  they have cultural dibs.  People mourn the gentrification of the San Francisco Mission, wailing about the destruction of a historically Latino community, not realizing that a hundred years ago the population was primarily Irish and Russian.  In LA, Watts was an integrated,  diverse community until it became majority black after WWII because of restrictive covenants elsewhere in the city.  The Castro became an LGBT haven when rights were largely denied,  but has become far more diverse in this century.  

All over our highly mobile nation, communities evolve over time.   When "us versus them" racial and ethnic thinking decline,  heterogeneous communities arise. 

Better to focus on social justice regardless of where people are living rather than try to hold back the tide to keep cultural sandcastles frozen in time.

comments.name: Tom Debley
comments.body:
There is something oddly appropriate about reviewing this “convention” as television, because television seems to have been its principal purpose. But that is also what troubles me about this piece.

We are examining the sideshow while paying too little attention to what the sideshow tells us about American politics.

There was no real convention here—no nominations, no ballots, no serious party business. Instead, we got hours of Donald Trump, grievance, attacks on political enemies and a crowd that seemed most energized by anger. At one point, a voice reportedly shouted that a Democratic candidate “should be shot.”

That deserves more than a review of whether the show had “oomph” or lost viewers to football.

Trump has spent years turning American politics into entertainment, and much of the press continues covering the performance because the performance is entertaining. But while we watch the carnival, something more consequential is happening behind the tent: a major political party is increasingly organized around one man, grievance is replacing governing, and political opponents are treated as enemies.

The First Amendment gives the press extraordinary freedom precisely because an informed citizenry is essential to democracy. Perhaps journalism's more important task now is not reviewing the sideshow, but helping Americans understand what the sideshow is distracting us from.

Yesterday I read the reporting about the now 25-year-old man whose mother died in the violence of 9 | 11. His grandmother apparently never cried in the child’s presence. That really seemed horrible to me. Let us grieve. Allow the grief to be felt. 

On the day, I remember saying to a friend, “Thus is going to result in so much more hate.” But then there seemed to be an inundation of goodwill to and for the United States—despite our history. Somehow it seemed that this barbaric event was going to transcend our history. 

“Never forget” and similar terse phrases that belie the nuances of why and how September 11th 2001 happened “to us.” I do cringe about the fetishization of what occurred on that pretty Tuesday morning and its aftermath. But I also periodically still feel grief for it all. 

And finally, I cannot believe are the byproduct of the conflagration continues to be referred to as “ash” or “dust”. That was non-nuclear fallout and no one ought to have concluded that it was anything but heartbreakingly and utterly toxic.

comments.name: W.B.

"...at her 116th birthday party, she couldn’t keep her eyes open,"

A shame you all had to bore an old lady like that.

Commenters: would you all be so querulous about death, if you didn't annually pantomime the odious personal holiday "BIRTH-DAY" that is imposed on practically every child in existence, who, by the way, didn't ask for it at all? 

When did you guys ever stop to think that maybe it was a literal waste of time? Effort? What the heck is with the morbid countdown?

And how many eating disorders did it kick off, one by one, plied with cake and ice cream by overbearing adults whose lip-licking enthusiasm is weirdly channeled for reasons not yet clear to the kids (that you're going to die, die, and DIE and not ever come back, and all too soon?)

Putting the consciousness of age, first and foremost, throughout your cultural practices, unconsciously, by rote and without compunction, this culture appropriated something (from somewhere, probably TV commercials) and forcibly merged it with our tenuous way of life, in the 1970s (before we went Hollywood). 

However, as the BIRTH-DAY rose inexorably in social intensity as touchstone and centerpiece of life's journey, the DEATH-DAY receded... the "Parlor" became a "Living Room" and it became an industry, not unlike Landscaping, where things are put away, in their proper places. 

From dirt, to dirt as the Book of Genesis says. *

comments.name: Alex
comments.body:
Prediction markets should be outlawed. The unavoidable problem is that they are far too easy to game. The major issue is insiders. Insiders will have an edge in predicting the outcome of wagers. More importantly and more consequentially, insiders may be in a position to influence the outcome, with potentially dangerous results. In the real world it is essentially impossible to police markets and identify many relevant insiders.

I don't worry much about insiders who obtain an unfair advantage. People participate in prediction markets voluntarily, and it has always been true and always will be true that fools and their money are soon parted.  I do however worry that insiders may influence outcomes in many consequential situations, sometimes to their financial advantage, but also possibly in public policy or even military situations.  Since prediction markets serve no useful function, the simplest solution is to ban them. 

As the article describes, prediction markets encourage excessive and addictive gambling, including among minors.

I also have serious concerns that some media organizations, such as Dow Jones, publisher of the Wall Street Journal, have chosen to sign partnerships with prediction markets. Frankly, this undermines the impartiality of their publications. These agreements represent a serious lapse in judgment.

My daughter always wanted to go to the park, but it was off limits, too many used needles and hookers turning tricks all day long in cars. She drew up a petition and she and my 6 year old daughter took it around and had everyone in the neighborhood sign it, they were mostly Chinese then.  She took the signed petition to the Commissioner of Parks.  The city immediately cleaned up the park and installed a playground.  My mom did Tai Chi with her neighbors for years after that.  She left the space to move onto our family farm in upstate New York.  If she was still with us today I'm sure she would buy the place.  So many  happy times there.

comments.name: D
comments.body:
My parents would have loved a more rural retirement. What kept them in their suburban home? Access to doctors and medical facilities.

Anyone who has had a child knows that a woman will want access to gynecologists, and will want a hospital with a maternity ward/NICU, then of course eighteen years of pediatric care.

Young families also prioritize things like decent schools that would have options for sports, clubs, music, and drama. 

Professionals are likely to need access to high speed, reliable Internet services.

What has been the trajectory for all of this in rural areas? The absolute wrong direction. Our profit centric health care “system” looks at specialists like ob/gyn, pediatric, and geriatric medicine providers as underutilized resources that don’t generate profit. Unless those doctors aren’t running wall to wall 15 minute sessions 40 hours a week they are not maximizing shareholder value. 

Rural schools struggle more than suburban ones (which certainly also have their own funding struggles), but the declining population has led to consolidation and shrinking of districts, as well as shrinking of programs.

Access to high speed Internet for rural areas has been something being pushed since the Clinton administration. Telcos have been given ridiculous amounts of money over the last 25 years in the spirit of previous electrification and telephone access programs, but the money has disappeared with poor results, and a bunch of self serving legislation.

comments.name: LT

There is something very on-brand for the GOP about rural counties spending thousands of dollars to attract working age residents while the federal government spends billions to keep immigrants out and deport some of those already here.
  
These communities need workers, taxpayers, and families to offset an aging population.
  
Instead of—or in addition to—paying people to move in and hoping they stay, we should make it possible for the immigrants already living and working there to remain legally.
  
Want to make rural America great again? Think of immigration as an economic resource, not the nightmare politicians paint to scare you.

comments.name: Patty
comments.body:
Perhaps if some of these rural places had invested in health and culture for their residents they may not have left. We live in a small, isolated place accessible only by ferry, boat, or air. We have no problem keeping and growing our population. We have a small, excellent health care facility, and art museum and theater. We have a community where people take care of each other. We pass taxes to conserve our beautiful place and the creatures that inhabit it. Our numerous small farms are mostly organic. We do not have even one traffic light.

Having a community that cares about its place and its residents is the key to maintaining (or growing) a population. A cheap house may be the holy grail initially, but when you can't find health care, pesticides are sprayed in those lovely spaces, schools dictate what you can and can't read, and neighbors view you with suspicion because you "aren't from here," people don't tend to stay.

The Ogala aquifer, underlying the central US, is being seriously depleted and climate change is expected to change the US prairies into desert.  The nation's breadbasket will move north into Canada. They know how to take the Long Island rail road and the subway, but they would rather hike the long trail. In our slice of heaven in Vermont, we have high speed fiber optic internet, Dartmouth and UVM healthcare services. We ski, golf, boat, play pickle ball, have great restaurants and farms. We have a beautiful public library and village green. We don’t plan anything around traffic except for ski season and no one cares what kind of handbags you have unless it’s really handy for carrying a dish for an impromptu dinner party. As others have noted, Kalshi and Polymarket are gambling sites, nothing more. The proof is in the fact that there are no deliverables.

Remember when oil futures went negative to the tune of negative $40 a barrel? That was because the storage system was crammed to capacity, and therefore oil had to be pumped to the end user (delivered) immediately. Anyone with an net positive position in oil futures faced the prospect of actually receiving physical oil. So because there is a deliverable, Oil futures concern a commodity, and are therefore subject to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

Kalshi and Polymarket, in contrast, have no deliverables. If you take on contract on what words Trump will use in a speech how many times, nobody will show up on your doorstep with a bag of words, win or lose.

Likewise, no one will plop a bound and gagged Maduro on your desk if he is not in office on a particular date. No deliverable.

Prediction markets are therefore gambling markets (I predict the Patriots will win, and I got $10 that says so), and need to be taxed and regulated accordingly.

So the next time someone tries to tell you that prediction markets are commodities markets and should be regulated by the CFTC and not the states, just bring up negative $40 oil and ask where are the deliverables in Kalshi or Polymarket. The silence will be deafening.

comments.name: John C

There are no deliverables in Kalshi or Polymarket, therefore they are not commodities markets and should not be subject to CFTC oversight. They are gambling sites, with stakes predicated on independent, third-party events. They should be taxed and regulated accordingly.

Just remember, oil hit negative $40 a barrel in the futures market because it is a deliverable. That makes it a commodity. The words spoken by the Angry Cheeto are not deliverables (nor to be believed, but that's a separate issue).

The achievements of ethnic and racial minorities in Japanese baseball are remarkable. Harimoto remains the only player to get 3,000 hits in Japan. Masaichi Kaneda, also an ethnic Korean, was the only pitcher to win 400 games. 

Career home run leader Sadaharu Oh is the son of a Japanese mother and Chinese father, and to this day remains a citizen of the Republic of China (aka Taiwan). Sachio Kinugasa, who played in 2,215 consecutive games from 1970 to 1987, was the son of a Japanese mother and African-American father. 

And the list goes on. Very interesting to see how ethnic Koreans in particular achieved success playing Japanese baseball in a manner similar to how African-Americans quickly became top stars in American baseball after Jackie Robinson broke the color barrier in 1947.
